claims: Behavior can reflect personal tendencies, circumstances, and their interaction.
Attribution biases describe tendencies rather than diagnoses of an individual.
1.note: A single late arrival cannot isolate character from circumstances. Use repeated observations and competing explanations; a bias label alone is not evidence.

claims: Random assignment improves comparisons between conditions; random sampling concerns who is selected.
One before-and-after difference does not isolate a cause; replication and uncertainty matter.
2.note: Random assignment helps balance other causes on average. It does not guarantee equal groups, prevent spillover, or make a narrow sample representative. The 12-versus-15 example is hypothetical and does not establish a reliable effect.

sources.title: Open Science Collaboration (2015), Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science

claims: Accessible examples can influence frequency judgments.
Representative records help distinguish a vivid impression from the underlying rate.
3.note: Heuristics can be useful. Diagnose a judgment by comparing it with relevant evidence, rather than assuming that an intuitive answer is biased. A complaint channel can identify faults without estimating their prevalence.

sources.title: Tversky & Kahneman (1973), Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability

claims: Dissonance is a theoretical framework; particular demonstrations need separate evaluation.
Irrecoverable costs differ from future costs and benefits.
4.note: The 2024 multilab study did not support its primary high-choice versus low-choice attitude prediction. That result concerns the tested induced-compliance procedure; it does not settle every dissonance claim. Past investments can still matter through their future consequences.

sources.title: Vaidis et al. (2024), A Multilab Replication of the Induced-Compliance Paradigm of Cognitive Dissonance
Arkes & Blumer (1985), The psychology of sunk cost

claims: Normative influence concerns acceptance; informational influence treats others as evidence.
Conformity, compliance, and obedience depend on the setting and process.
5.note: The classic tasks used particular participants, procedures, and pressures. Their results should not be converted into a universal conformity or obedience rate. Independent judgments and stop rules are practical hypotheses to evaluate in a real group.

claims: Motivation and ability influence how much a message is examined.
Descriptive and injunctive norms concern behavior and approval respectively.
6.note: Central and peripheral processing describe differences along an elaboration continuum. A cue can matter in more than one way depending on the decision. A click, an attitude report, informed participation, and sustained behavior are different outcomes.

sources.title: Elaboration Likelihood Model, Oxford reference entry
Cialdini, Reno & Kallgren (1990), A focus theory of normative conduct

claims: Group polarization, social loafing, and coordination loss describe different processes.
An unfinished task is insufficient evidence that people are loafing.
7.note: A poor decision does not establish groupthink, and poor output does not establish low effort. Identify an observable process before choosing a remedy. The café examples illustrate possible explanations rather than diagnosing real groups.

sources.title: Karau & Williams (1993), Social loafing: A meta-analytic review and theoretical integration

claims: Stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination are distinct, related concepts.
Contact interventions and procedural changes need outcome-based evaluation.
8.note: Contact is not a universal remedy. The 2019 review found important gaps in randomized evidence for particular adult prejudice outcomes; the 2021 review also highlights limits in durability and generalization. Evaluate the actual population, setting, access, behavior, and follow-up. A single implicit-association score is not a character diagnosis.

sources.title: Paluck, Green & Green (2019), The contact hypothesis re-evaluated
Paluck et al. (2021), Prejudice Reduction: Progress and Challenges
sources.kind: Review of intervention experiments; abstract available

claims: Opportunity, familiarity, and similarity can be associated with liking and connection.
Disclosure and perceived responsiveness can contribute to experienced intimacy.
9.note: Repeated exposure is not an unlimited rule that more contact produces more liking. Meta-analytic patterns vary with conditions and can be nonlinear. Relationship associations do not establish a guaranteed intervention, and they never override a person’s boundary.

sources.title: Montoya et al. (2017), A re-examination of the mere exposure effect
Laurenceau, Barrett & Pietromonaco (1998), Intimacy as an interpersonal process

claims: Bystander effects depend on danger, relationships, and available support.
Aggression measures and helping plans require careful interpretation.
10.note: Other people can reduce an individual’s likelihood of helping in some settings and provide essential support in others. A crowd is not a deterministic cause of inaction. Social-psychology models do not replace emergency training, and laboratory aggression measures are imperfect indicators of serious violence.

sources.title: Fischer et al. (2011), The bystander-effect: a meta-analytic review
